s04.slug: MONDAY · 3:30 PM · STATE STREET, SANTA BARBARA — TIDEWATER BOOKS
body: The afternoon is gold over the water when the Saab comes down off the 101 at the beach, and by then he has told her “The Dead.” She made him, on the on-ramp at Marisol, because she has never read it and wouldn’t let him summarize, so he told it properly, start to finish: the old aunts’ party in the snow, Freddy Malins turning up drunk, Gabriel and his galoshes and the speech he keeps rehearsing, Miss Ivors calling him a West Briton in the middle of a dance and leaving before the supper he was about to carve the goose for; the tenor with a cold singing on the stairs, and Gretta stopped on the landing to listen; the Gresham Hotel, and the boy in the rain. She drove with both hands on the wheel and interrupted twice, once to ask what galoshes were and once to say, about Gabriel, “Oh, I *hate* him,” with real pleasure.

body.text: At the light on Cabrillo she leans across and puts her nose to the collar of the Carhartt. “You had one.” “One.” She sits back and asks him what a gasworks is.

body: Coming up State he tells her why it has to be a store. Trumbull takes books only from a seller, shipped in the seller’s box, nothing handed over by family; in the fall *Brideshead* went to Danny by way of Driftwood, and the C.O. who read it first reported that it was about a house. And he tells her that before Christmas Danny walked into the prison library and asked for Flannery O’Connor, because Jack wouldn’t shut up about her across a visiting-room table. They had one story of hers, in an anthology with the cover torn off: the grandmother. Danny wrote Ma afterward that she raised peacocks and she was mean and he liked her.
“Then he’s getting the rest of her,” Skye says, and changes lanes without signaling, her version of applause.

February on State Street is seventy degrees and a little embarrassed about it: the sun along the arcades, the red tile warm to look at, a man in shorts walking a bulldog in a sweater. She parks below Carrillo in front of a meter with a dent in its head and holds out her hand, palm up. Jack puts four quarters in it. She feeds them in one at a time, watches the little red flag drop out of sight, and says, “See? I keep my promises.”
On the sidewalk she takes his arm. “Was it about the dog?”
Somebody’s version of Wednesday has made it out to Del Playa, and from the question, the version had a dog in it.
“Mostly the dog,” Jack says.
She looks at him over the top of her sunglasses for about as long as it takes a car to pass. Then she pushes them back up. “Good dog,” she says, and holds the door.

Tidewater Books is a shoebox stood on its end and pushed back from the street: narrow, deep, dim after the sidewalk, shelves to the pressed-tin ceiling and a library ladder on a brass rail to reach the top of them. A gray cat is asleep on the new hardcovers in a square of window. Behind the register, on a little stereo between a spike of receipts and a jar of pens, two acoustic guitars and a boy’s voice, sweet and very young, are coming from some year before either of them was born. The man at the register has a gray ponytail and a paperback, and he nods at them over it.
“He’s not mine,” he says, when Skye crouches to the cat. “He comes in for the window.”

She won’t let Jack help. She goes down the fiction wall on her knees with her head tipped sideways to read the spines, past the M’s and the N’s, and comes up out of the O’s with it: *The Complete Stories*, fat as a phone book, the spine never cracked. She holds it up over her head at him from the floor.
“He’s read the grandmother,” she says. “Now he gets the rest of the family.”

The man with the ponytail takes the shipping without a blink. They send to Lompoc every week, he says; once, to Folsom. He slides a form across, and Jack fills it in in his ordinary hand, the name and the number and the institution and the town, and takes a ten-pack of envelopes off the rack by the register while he’s at it, the glossy kind, because they’re there.
“Gift?” the man says.
“It’s for his brother,” Skye says. “He’s in Ohio.”
*Ohio*. Jack notices the word she picked.

No wrapping, the man tells her, no card, nothing taped inside; they open everything. She can write on the packing slip if she wants. She wants. She takes a pen out of the jar and turns her shoulder to Jack and writes in her block letters, fast, and he gets the top line before she folds it — FOR DANNY, 23. — and then the rest goes under the fold and inside the front cover, and she settles the book in its box with both hands, like she’s tucking it in.
“What’d you write?”
“Things,” she says. “Professional things.”

While the man tapes it, she drifts back to fiction and comes out with a Penguin *Dubliners* off the shelf, and stands in the aisle reading the last pages with one finger going down the margin and her lips moving. The boy on the stereo has gone on to something else. Jack leans on the end of the shelf and doesn’t interrupt her, which is harder than it sounds.
She closes it on her finger. “Okay. Gretta.”
“Gabriel.”

“No. *Gretta*.” She ticks them off on the *Dubliners*. “The aunts are doing hostess. Freddy’s doing drunk. Miss Ivors is doing Ireland. And Gabriel is doing everything — the galoshes, the speech, the quote he’s worried is too smart for the room. He’s running lines in his head all through the party. I’ve worked with that guy. I’ve *been* that guy, at a lot of parties.” She opens the book again. “And she’s on the stairs, listening to a song and thinking about a dead boy. She’s the only person in the house who’s actually where she is. He looks up and sees her and wants to paint her. He’s got a title for it. *Distant Music*.” She shuts it. “Then he gets her to the hotel with plans, and finds out the night was hers and he was background.”

“And then it snows,” Jack says. “On everybody. On the living and the dead, on the boy’s grave out in the west, on Gabriel at the window. It’s the first time all night he isn’t the middle of anything. He just gets to be one of the people it’s falling on. It comes from outside, it covers everybody, and he didn’t earn a flake of it.” He shrugs inside the Carhartt. “That’s grace. It doesn’t care who gave the speech.”
She reads it to him off the page, quietly, so the man at the register can’t hear her doing it — *falling faintly through the universe and faintly falling* — and looks up.

“*I think he died for me*,” she says. “She says that to her husband in a hotel room. You can’t act that line. It’s a terrible reading. It’s just true.” She taps the last page. “He got *cast*, Jack. He spent all night auditioning for the lead, and at the end somebody finally tells him he’s the husband in a story about a boy who stood in the rain. It’s a smaller part. And it’s the first time all night he’s right for it.” She smiles at him over the book. “You can call that grace if you want. In my business it’s called getting the note.”

response: She laughs out loud in the fiction aisle, and the cat that isn’t anybody’s gets down off the hardcovers and leaves.
“Yes,” she says. “And it doesn’t take meetings.” She points the *Dubliners* at him. “But that’s mine. You’re doing my material at me. Point to me.”
He gives her the point. She puts Joyce back on the shelf spine-in, so the next person has to want it.

choices.text: “You’re right. He’s the only one acting.”
response: She holds the book against her chest and studies him a while, long enough for the boy on the stereo to finish a song.
“Don’t concede to me in a bookstore,” she says. “I’ll get used to it.”

She carries the *Dubliners* up to the register and buys it too, and has the man put it in a bag, not the box. “That one’s mine,” she tells him. “I’m going to read it with a pencil and find out I was right.”
She opens her mouth to win and, for a second, has nothing in it.

Then she does. “Then I’ve been in the wrong business,” she says, and backs him two steps into the Penguin Classics by the front of the Carhartt and kisses him, short and thorough, the *Dubliners* still open in her other hand against his back. Somewhere behind him a row of spines gives a little.
At the end of the aisle a woman with a canvas tote comes around the corner, stops, and reverses out politely the way she came.

s04a.slug: MONDAY · 4:35 PM · STATE STREET AT CARRILLO — THE RED LIGHT
body: She puts the top down outside Tidewater — the latch over the mirror, the button, the canvas folding itself back into the trunk in sections — and by Carrillo the sun is low enough to come in sideways between the buildings and lie across their laps. She’s in her gray fleece zipped to the chin and her sunglasses, her hair knotted up off her neck with a pen from the store’s jar she didn’t give back. The paper bag with his envelopes rides in the back seat. The box stayed on the counter for the UPS man, and the receipt is in Jack’s jeans with his brother’s number on it in his own hand.
The light at Carrillo goes red and she stops first in line, under a palm with a shopping cart parked at its foot.
“Danny’s twenty-three tomorrow,” Jack says.
“What do you get for twenty-three in there?”

“A phone call. Push-ups. Ma puts money on his account and he buys honey buns off the commissary sheet.” He puts his head back on the seat. “Out here you don’t get anything either. Twenty-five you get the car insurance. Twenty-three’s a layover.”

Skye watches the light. “I had my sixteenth on a soundstage in Burbank,” she says. “They wheeled out a sheet cake at lunch with my character’s name on it. Not mine. Hers. They spelled it right.” She lifts one shoulder. “I ate the corner with the most frosting. It’s a sickness.”
“Danny got his name on a cake every year till he left,” Jack says. “Ma’s handwriting. She always ran out of room before the *y* and had to go up the side.”
“So he’s been Dann his whole life.”
“With a *y* up the side.”
She takes that in like it’s a fact she’s going to need later, and nods.

The radio has been an LA station since they got in the car, fading on the curves and coming back, and it comes back now out of an ad for a mattress store and, unasked, plays it: the slow synth, the heartbeat drum, the falsetto easing in like it has all night. Skye reaches over and turns it up as far as it goes, and turns in her seat to look at him.
“It’s a *sign*,” she says.
“*An evil and adulterous generation seeks a sign*,” Jack says.
“Then we’re the target audience.”

She takes the first verse. She has every word of it, and she gives it to him, not to the street and not to the car beside them: to him, eyes on his, conducting with a lime out of the cup holder. Her sunglasses go up into her hair on a high note and end up crooked and she leaves them that way. Jack has the hook from the far side of a cinderblock wall — Doug Pruitt plays this song at one in the morning more often than a man should, and Jack has lain in 412 and learned it against his will — and when it comes around he’s there for it, drumming the dash with both hands, and they hit it together at the top of their lungs, straight at each other, their eyes never leaving each other’s, in daylight, on State Street: “*Birthday sex* —”
A woman coming out of the bank on the corner with her deposit slip stops on the curb to watch.

In the turn lane beside them a silver Jetta has its windows down. In the passenger seat a college girl in a UCSB sweatshirt has her iPhone up at arm’s length, laughing so hard it shakes, pointed at them. Jack sees the phone. Skye, mid-verse, waves the lime at the Jetta like the grand marshal of something and doesn’t drop a word.

Somewhere in the second verse he thinks, very clearly, *Danny would pay money for this*, and then Skye leans across the gearshift and sings the next line with her mouth at his ear, and he loses the thought, and doesn’t miss it.
The light is still red. The verse runs out, and the hook is coming back around, and she points the lime at him: his.

choices.text: *Stand up in your seat for the hook.*
choices.key: At a red light on State Street, the day before Danny’s birthday, you stood up in the Saab and sang it at her.
response: He stands up in the passenger seat with one hand on the windshield frame and gives the hook to State Street — to the bank and the palm and the shopping cart and the girl in the Jetta. Skye is laughing too hard to sing and conducts him anyway, with the lime, from below. A man outside the bank puts down his briefcase to applaud.
The light goes green with Jack still standing. She floors it, and he sits down hard in the leather with the song still going, laughing, his hand still up in the air where the windshield was.

choices.key: At a red light on State Street, the day before Danny’s birthday, you did the high part — badly, at her, at the top of your lungs.
response: The falsetto, which he does not have, at full commitment, with his eyes shut and his hand on his heart for the anthem. Something comes out of him that the radio did not put there.

Skye has to stop singing to laugh, and then can’t start again. She folds over the wheel with the lime in her fist and her sunglasses sliding the rest of the way out of her hair, and every time she gets her breath back he does another bar of it at her, and she goes again.
The light changes, and the car behind them honks, not unkindly, twice.

choices.text: *Sing it to her and nobody else.*
choices.key: At a red light on State Street, the day before Danny’s birthday, you sang it to her and nobody else.
response: He turns all the way in his seat, one knee up on the leather, and sings it to her — every line he knows, straight at her, not loud now, the radio carrying the rest. It’s a ridiculous song, and he doesn’t sing it like one.
She stops conducting. The lime sits in her open hand on the gearshift. She takes the sunglasses down out of her hair and holds them, and doesn’t put them on.
The light changes. She doesn’t notice until the Jetta goes.
